The shares closed on November 6 just 1.2% below their high for the year. Following a run like that, shareholders want to know what might slow the stock down. Management pointed to a specific headwind during the company’s October 30 earnings call, naming a pressure that begins in 2027. What is that pressure, and has AbbVie felt it before? During the fiscal Q3 2026 call, management said the IRA price for the psychiatry drug Vraylar will begin in 2027, and instructed analysts to build it into their models. Under a U.S. drug-pricing law known as the IRA, the government can select certain drugs and publish prices for them. Management did not specify on the call how much of Vraylar’s sales will face that price impact. AbbVie has encountered this before. Sales of the cancer drug Imbruvica fell 26.1% in fiscal Q3 2026, a decline management attributed to IRA pricing and competitive share pressure. Imbruvica’s revenue had already dropped 6.9% in fiscal 2024 and 14.3% in fiscal 2025. Vraylar is the next AbbVie drug management has named, even as it continues to grow. Global sales of the treatment reached nearly $1.1 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, marking an increase of 14.3%. In fiscal 2025, Vraylar sales rose 10.8% from a year earlier to $3.62 billion. That performance accounted for 5.9% of the company’s revenue for the year. Management expects the drug to reach $4.2 billion in sales for fiscal 2026, so the drug is still adding sales right up to the year its price begins. Botox remains an open question. Sales of Botox Therapeutic climbed 14.8% to $3.77 billion in fiscal 2025, making it slightly larger than Vraylar. During the call, management argued the IRA cannot select Botox because human serum albumin, one of its three ingredients, derives from human blood plasma. A federal district court ruled in AbbVie’s favor on that point the day before the call. The company added that the matter is not over since the government can still appeal, and management noted it does not expect a price to be published while that plays out. Investors are currently paying a high price for AbbVie’s earnings. The stock trades at 49.8 times its last twelve months of earnings, compared with 21.8 for the S&P 500. That valuation relies on reported earnings, which run well below the company’s adjusted measure. During fiscal Q3 2026, AbbVie recorded $2.37 a share under its reported measure, alongside an adjusted figure of $3.82 a share. While the IRA price presents a real cost, it has reached AbbVie one drug at a time so far, and the company has kept growing through the first one. Total revenue rose 10.3% in fiscal Q3 2026, even as Imbruvica’s sales shrank. Management said that many sell-side models already appear to include the Vraylar price, and the company expects top-tier growth again in 2027. AbbVie stock has also fallen less than the S&P 500 during most recent market shocks. The shares dropped 13.0% in the 2025 tariff shock, compared with a 19.0% decline for the index. During the 2022 inflation shock, the stock shed 1.5%, while the index fell 24.0%. The 2023 banking crisis stood as an exception, with AbbVie falling 13.0% as the S&P 500 fell 6.7%. title: Why Should AbbVie Stock Holders Watch This One Number? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. AbbVie (ABBV) now draws nearly half of its sales from two drugs. Out of $17.4 billion in total revenue during the third quarter of 2026, the company sold $8.48 billion of Skyrizi and Rinvoq, its two biggest immunology treatments. For a holder, this concentration makes AbbVie stock largely a bet on those two products. So why is AbbVie relying on those two drugs more than it did a year ago? AbbVie relies more heavily on these two drugs because they are growing more than twice as fast as the company as a whole. Skyrizi sales reached nearly $5.8 billion in the third quarter, rising 22.9% on an operational basis that excludes currency moves. Rinvoq sales climbed 24.3% on the same basis, while AbbVie’s total revenue grew 10.5%, also excluding currency. Management gave its reasons during the October 30 call, saying that both drugs continue to beat its expectations and that Skyrizi still wins roughly 1 out of every 2 new or switching psoriasis patients. Humira, another AbbVie immunology drug, is moving the other way. Its sales fell 30.6% to $683 million, a decline management put down to continued biosimilar competition, meaning cheaper copies of the drug. With the two drugs outpacing AbbVie overall while Humira shrinks, Skyrizi and Rinvoq now account for a larger share of AbbVie’s sales than they did a year ago. Other AbbVie drugs illustrate what can cut into a major product’s sales. Humira is not the only treatment losing sales. Imbruvica, a cancer drug, saw its sales fall 26.1% in the third quarter. Management put this drop down to competitive pressure on its market share and to IRA pricing, which was set under a U.S. drug price law. Management also said the IRA price for Vraylar, its psychiatry drug, begins in 2027. Skyrizi and Rinvoq face rivals as well. Management said on the call that the two drugs have been on the market for 8 years and now encounter more competition, including recent oral competition for Skyrizi in psoriasis. Management also said this oral competition is not having a substantive impact on Skyrizi’s share of new patients. Evidence pointing the other way centers on new uses. On October 23, 2026, the FDA approved an under-the-skin starting dose of Skyrizi for Crohn’s disease, an addition management expects will lift Skyrizi’s share of new Crohn’s patients over the next several quarters. Management also expects U.S. approvals of Rinvoq for vitiligo and alopecia areata over the next several months, estimating that these two uses will generate nearly $2 billion of peak sales together. AbbVie has raised its Skyrizi sales guidance for 2026 three times. AbbVie stock trades at 7.7 times sales, compared with 3.3 for the S&P 500. The shares returned 37.5% in the year to November 5, 2026, against 9.9% for the index. The price likely assumes that Skyrizi and Rinvoq will keep growing well ahead of the rest of the company. The stock has not always held up better than the market when trouble arrived. During the 2023 regional banking crisis, AbbVie fell 13.0% while the S&P 500 fell 6.7%. In the 2022 inflation shock, the stock fell only 1.5% while the index fell 24.0%. Each shock picks different winners, which is why building for a crash and a rally beats guessing. A holder should take this reliance seriously, but not as an alarm: for now, Skyrizi and Rinvoq are among AbbVie’s fastest-growing drugs, not its weak spots. For the risk to be worth taking, both drugs need to keep winning new patients as competition grows, enough to make up for Humira’s falling sales. AbbVie is expected to report its fourth quarter in February 2027, and plans to give its 2027 guidance on that call. Adjusted earnings per share came in comfortably, even after absorbing a charge for acquired in-process research and milestone payments, which management always includes in its results because they come with its business development approach. The company then raised its adjusted earnings per share range for the full year, narrowing and lifting the band. That range already embeds the year-to-date research charges, which is a useful reminder that guidance for this company is not a clean operating number but one burdened by deal-related expense. Posted earnings sit well below adjusted earnings, as is typical for a group with heavy intangible amortization after earlier large acquisitions. Immunology remains the heart of the enterprise. Skyrizi and Rinvoq each grew at a strong double-digit pace, and together they now generate far more revenue than Humira did at the point when its decline began to be noticeable. Humira itself fell sharply, the expected consequence of biosimilar erosion in the United States and elsewhere. That arithmetic is the core of the capital spending narrative. Years ago, analysts feared that Humira's patent cliff would leave a gaping hole. Instead, the company engineered a replacement cycle with new molecules, broader labels and aggressive launch execution. The latest quarter shows the replacement not only complete in revenue terms but also still growing. A further regulatory milestone arrived with approval of a subcutaneous induction option for Skyrizi in Crohn's disease, which may simplify treatment initiation for patients and physicians. Neuroscience grew faster than the group average, reflecting sizeable contributions from Vraylar, Botox in therapeutic uses, the migraine pair Ubrelvy and Qulipta, and the Parkinson's disease therapy Vyalev. Each product addresses a chronic condition with durable demand, so the segment adds a layer of stability beneath the more cyclical immunology story. The regulatory calendar also helped. A new Parkinson's option based on tavapadon received approval, expanding the company's presence in movement disorders. Such additions matter because they reduce reliance on any single molecule and give the sales force broader conversations with neurologists. Diversification is a standing theme in pharma dividend analysis. Not every line advanced. Aesthetics edged lower overall, with the toxin franchise growing modestly while the dermal filler brand declined. Consumer-funded procedures respond to confidence and discretionary spending, and competitive launches in filler have added pressure. The company has described aesthetics as a recovery story that depends on consumer sentiment normalising. Oncology was nearly flat. Venclexta and Elahere contributed meaningful sales, but the older Imbruvica franchise continued to erode due to competition and regulatory price effects. These softer areas show why a single strong quarter is not a guarantee. Moves of this kind are often read against the wider S&P 500. For AbbVie

title: What Could AbbVie Stock Be Worth In Three Years? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. AbbVie (ABBV) stock returned 40.6% in the year to November 4, 2026, against 14.9% for the S&P 500. You may hold it after that run or be thinking of buying. Either way, the company’s profit is hard to project because AbbVie’s net income more than quadrupled in the twelve months to September 2026 from a year earlier. So what would a share bought today be worth if AbbVie keeps growing? Based on AbbVie’s own figures, a scenario shows that a share bought at $294.83 on November 4, 2026, would be worth about $328.03 three years later. That represents an 11.3% upside before dividends. In that scenario, sales grow 9.1% a year, a rate that equals 85% of AbbVie’s latest twelve-month pace of 10.7%. The net margin ends at a blend of 70% of today’s level and 30% of its average at the twelve quarter ends before the latest one. The P/E stays at today’s level. This multiple sits below its 69.5 average at ten quarter ends from December 2023 to September 2026, leaving out readings above 100. The share count stays at today’s level. AbbVie’s diluted count rose about 0.06% over the three years to September 2026, and if that pattern went on, each share would get slightly less. Here is how AbbVie today compares with the scenario three years on. Higher sales produce all of the gain, though the scenario’s lower net margin offsets part of it. None of the upside comes from the P/E. Most of AbbVie’s sales growth comes from its immunology drugs, led by Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Immunology revenue approached $9.2 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, up 16.6% on an operational basis. On its October 30, 2026 call, management said it expects to deliver top-tier growth again in 2027. Management also said Skyrizi and Rinvoq are adding about $6 billion of sales combined in 2026, even with more competition. Skyrizi alone sold $17.6 billion in fiscal 2025, an increase of 49.9% from a year earlier. Those gains have to keep outrunning AbbVie’s losses elsewhere. Humira sales fell 30.6% in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, to $683 million. Management put this decline down to continued competition from biosimilar copies. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue outlook to about $67.8 billion. Three of that year’s quarters are already reported, so the outlook is mostly results already in hand, not a pace for later years. How AbbVie’s Upside Changes Under Other Assumptions Each row below changes one assumption while keeping the other two as they are in the scenario. The scenario bases its sales growth on AbbVie’s fastest pace of the past three years. Twelve-month revenue growth was 0.7% in the period to September 2024 and 7.4% a year later. Today’s net margin is also nearly twice its average at the twelve quarter ends from September 2023 to June 2026, so the margin in the scenario is set lower. Taken one at a time, three years of owning AbbVie stock would return nothing, before dividends, if revenue growth slowed to 5.3% a year. That compares with 10.7% in the twelve months to September 2026. Owning the stock would also return nothing if the net margin fell to 12.1% in year three, against 15.7% today. The same holds if the P/E fell to 45.3, against 50.4 at the November 4, 2026 close. AbbVie’s twelve-month net margin is the measure to watch when the company reports its fiscal fourth quarter, expected in February 2027. After a run like this, the hard questions are personal: hold, trim or sell, and the tax on each.
